concepts.decision: Select channel controls from data/media, threat, endpoint trust, duration, and operational need.
concepts.definition: Communication path with defined endpoints, identity, protection, authorization, monitoring, failure behavior, and lifecycle governance.
concepts.failureExample: An encrypted channel to an unmanaged endpoint exposes data after decryption.
concepts.label: Secure Channel

concepts.decision: Require MFA, managed endpoint/jump/broker, least privilege, session evidence, time bounds, and revocation.
concepts.definition: Privileged or user remote connection to internal resources through an approved, authenticated, scoped path.
concepts.failureExample: A vendor keeps permanent remote administrator access after maintenance ends.
concepts.label: Remote Access

concepts.decision: Govern participant admission, encryption endpoints, recording/screen-share authority, retention, client updates, and moderation.
concepts.definition: Protection of live media, chat/files, recordings, transcripts, rooms/devices, and collaboration identity/authorization.
concepts.failureExample: A meeting is encrypted but an unauthorized participant records sensitive screens.
concepts.label: Voice Video Security

concepts.decision: Define boundary, identity, least privilege, route/data protection, logs, notification, support window, contract, and exit.
concepts.definition: Network or support access involving an external carrier, supplier, hardware vendor, or partner.
concepts.failureExample: A provider support tunnel remains active with shared credentials and no logs.
concepts.label: Third Party Connectivity

concepts.decision: Choose endpoint identity, selectors/split routing, device posture, logging, key lifecycle, and termination/authorization boundary.
concepts.definition: Tunnel that protects selected traffic between defined endpoints across an untrusted/intermediate network.
concepts.failureExample: A VPN user can route to every subnet because selectors and authorization are broad.
concepts.label: VPN

concepts.decision: Validate certificate/hostname, locate termination, manage versions/keys, and protect upstream/downstream paths.
concepts.definition: Application-session protection between authenticated TLS endpoints.
concepts.failureExample: TLS ends at a proxy and traffic to an internal service is unprotected.
concepts.label: TLS

concepts.decision: Use approved jump paths, host-key verification, least privilege, logging, session control, and credential/key lifecycle.
concepts.definition: Secure remote administrative/session transport with host and user authentication.
concepts.failureExample: An administrator accepts a changed host key and sends commands to an impostor.
concepts.label: Ssh

concepts.decision: Assess encryption endpoint, provider boundary, resiliency, monitoring, jurisdiction, and fallback.
concepts.definition: Transport connecting access/edge sites to core/provider services, often with carrier, capacity, route, and latency dependencies.
concepts.failureExample: A single carrier backhaul outage isolates remote sites despite local redundancy.
concepts.label: Backhaul

misconceptions.claim: A VPN makes remote users trusted by default.
misconceptions.correction: The VPN is one channel control; identity, device posture, authorization, segmentation, monitoring, and session limits still determine trust.

misconceptions.claim: A provider's encrypted link removes the need for contractual controls.
misconceptions.correction: Contracts define roles, support access, data handling, notification, evidence, and termination that encryption cannot provide.

outcome: Choose and operate a secure channel for voice/video, remote administration, data transport, or third-party connectivity while preserving identity, confidentiality, integrity, availability, and accountability.

sections.body: Voice, video, and collaboration platforms need identity assurance, meeting admission, authorization, encryption appropriate to the threat, recording and screen-sharing governance, secure clients, updates, and logging. Remote administrative access needs strong authentication, least privilege, managed endpoints, approved jump paths, session controls, and separation from ordinary user traffic. Convenience features should not silently expand the trust boundary.
keyPoints: A secure session includes endpoint, identity, channel, content, and administrative controls.
Remote administration is a high-value path and should be isolated, monitored, and time-bounded.
Meeting recordings, chat, transcripts, and shared screens become governed information assets.
sections.title: Protect people and administrators

sections.body: Backhaul, satellite, carrier, telecom, hardware-support, and other third-party channels require defined service boundaries, route and data protection, authentication, availability expectations, incident notification, logging, access expiry, and contractual accountability. Select VPN, TLS, SSH, or other protections by layer and use case; verify that encryption endpoints and metadata exposure match the threat model.
keyPoints: A provider relationship does not eliminate the customer's responsibility for data, identities, and configuration.
Third-party connectivity should be narrowly scoped, monitored, and revocable.
Availability and latency requirements influence channel and cryptographic choices.
sections.title: Govern data paths and external dependencies

sections.body: Voice, video, and collaboration channels create live media plus recordings, transcripts, chat, files, and metadata; govern identity, room/device posture, encryption, recording authorization, retention, and moderation. Remote administrative access needs brokered identity, MFA, least privilege, jump paths, time bounds, session evidence, and revocation. Data communications such as backhaul and satellite require availability, latency, provider, jurisdiction, encryption endpoint, and fallback decisions. Third-party telecom and hardware support requires contracts, access windows, support identities, monitoring, incident duties, and exit evidence.
keyPoints: Transport encryption does not govern stored collaboration artifacts or endpoint trust.
A channel's availability and provider dependency can be as important as confidentiality.
Third-party support should be treated as a controlled identity and data path, not permanent trust.
sections.title: Choose channel controls for collaboration, remote, data, and third-party paths

learningJob.plainExplanation: A secure channel requires authorized purpose, named identity and device, constrained actions, observation, revocation, and verified closure. A live-channel property does not automatically protect stored recordings, copied scripts, or lingering accounts.
learningJob.visualReasoningGain: A vendor-session swimlane adds lifecycle accountability; a channel-versus-artifact table would extend the reasoning to voice, video, data, and stored copies.
